# A Practical Project Intake Process: Four Gates Before Work Enters the Portfolio

Use a four-gate project intake framework to capture comparable requests, test feasibility, and make clear portfolio decisions before work begins.

August 18, 2026·8 min read

## Project intake should produce a decision, not just collect requests

Project intake should answer a practical question before anyone starts building a schedule: should this request become portfolio work now, later, after revision, or not at all? A request form by itself cannot answer that question. It collects information, but it does not establish what evidence is sufficient, who evaluates it, or what decision follows.

A useful intake process is a decision-quality system. It gathers enough comparable evidence to test whether a request is complete, aligned, feasible, and viable beside existing commitments. Detailed planning comes after the appropriate decision, not before every idea has consumed delivery effort.

This article recommends a lightweight four-gate framework for PMO and operations leaders. It is not a formal PMO standard or an implementation of a named commercial methodology. PMI guidance supports using a defined governance framework rather than an inconsistent approach. Stage-gate methods generally distinguish work stages from decision gates where leaders evaluate whether work should continue, change direction, or stop. The number of gates, evidence required, review cadence, and approval authority should fit your organization’s size, risk profile, and funding model.

## Use a minimum intake record that makes requests comparable

The intake record is not a complete business case, project charter, or delivery plan. It is a concise record that lets reviewers compare one request with another without asking every requester to produce a detailed work breakdown structure or committed budget. Portfolio-management guidance commonly separates proposal development, selection, prioritization, and registration of approved work. That separation matters because the evidence needed to qualify a request is different from the evidence needed to execute it.
## Run four gates before you commit portfolio capacity

The four gates below are a recommended framework. They set an evidence threshold appropriate to the decision at hand rather than demanding a complete execution plan during the first review. In a small organization, one operations leader may perform most of the review. In a larger organization, PMO triage, functional review, and a leadership decision forum may own different gates.

A Compliance Signoff is an attributable attestation: a named, accountable party formally certifies, on a durable record, that the legal, regulatory, safety, or policy criteria governing a step have been satisfied — and that any deviations have been logged as explicit exceptions — before the step is allowed to proceed. 
## How it implements the components¶

Compliance Signoff fills the accountability-and-record side of the archetype:

  * `evidence_packet` — the certification points at the compiled proof (control tests, reconciliations, findings) that the criteria were met.
  * `gate_authority` — the named, accountable signer whose personal certification is the sanctioned act that lets the step proceed.
  * `audit_trail` — the durable, attributable record of criteria, evidence, signature, timing, and exceptions; the mechanism's anchor and reason for existing.
  * `exception_override_policy` — deviations are handled as governed waivers with owner, justification, and expiry, rather than being passed silently.

It does not itself define the stage boundary or the real-time readiness bar (`stage_gate`, `readiness_criteria` — that is Clinical Clearance Protocol), and it does not recalibrate the criteria over time (`criteria_revision_cadence` — that is Educational Mastery Assessment); a compliance signoff certifies and records that a given rule set was met.

# Systems assurance on rail: linking design maturity to construction readiness

3 min read · Dr. Sriniwasa Prabhu N · Founder & Managing Director · Project Assure · 2026

On complex rail programmes the most dangerous risk is the one nobody owns: a design milestone reported complete that does not actually make the next package ready to build.

In short

On multi-contract rail programmes, a design package marked complete only means a document was issued; it does not mean the downstream package can start. Independent systems assurance ties each design milestone to demonstrable readiness through a stage-gate assessment covering requirements traceability, interface control across contracts, and readiness criteria at each gate.

Large rail programmes fail at the seams. Individual contracts can each report themselves on track while the interfaces between them quietly slip, because design milestones are treated as paperwork events rather than as gates to real construction readiness.

## Why does a design package marked complete not mean the next package is ready?

A design package marked complete tells you a document was issued. It does not tell you whether the downstream package can actually start: whether interfaces are resolved, approvals secured, and requirements verified. On a multi-contract programme, that gap between complete and ready is where unacknowledged risk accumulates, invisible until it surfaces as a delay nobody planned for.

## How does stage-gate assessment link design milestones to construction readiness?

Independent systems assurance closes the gap by tying each design milestone to demonstrable readiness through a stage-gate assessment:

  * Traceability from requirements through design to verification, so nothing is assumed closed that is still open.
  * Interface control across contracts, so the seams are owned rather than left between scopes.
  * Readiness criteria at each gate, a package advances only when the work it enables can genuinely begin.

> Assurance is not a report issued at handover. It is a continuous, evidence-based process that makes readiness (and the risk of its absence) visible while there is still time to act.

## What the Stage Gate Process Must Test, Gate by Gate

The most common corruption of a stage gate process is testing documents instead of evidence. “The business case exists” is a document test: it passes anything with a cover page. “The benefits in the business case have baselines, and named owners agreed to them in writing” is an evidence test: it fails most of what the first test passes. Every gate in the sequence below is built on that distinction.

## Key Takeaways

  * A stage gate process only governs when all three outcomes (proceed, recycle, kill) happen in practice. The gate log, not the framework document, is the proof.
  * Gates test evidence, not documents: baselined benefits with named owners, working output demonstrated, rehearsed cutovers. Every criterion must be observable.
  * The gatekeeper is never the team being gated, and the gatekeeper’s authority must match the decision the gate exists to make.
  * A pass rate at or near 100 percent is the clearest single sign of gate theater. Count kills, recycles, and closed conditions before trusting any gate system.
  * Rigor should scale with project size and risk: merge gates by combining their questions for small projects, never by dropping a question outright.
  * A genuine recycle costs weeks; a genuine kill caught at a mid-delivery gate avoids months of compounding a business case that has quietly stopped being true.
  * Regulated or statutory gates need genuine authority to say no, sequenced early enough that saying no is still a cheap decision: inserted late, they become structurally extracted rather than free.

A Stage-Gate Review chops a project into phases and installs a decision point at every boundary, where an authorized gatekeeper — separate from the delivery team — decides whether current evidence justifies authorizing the next phase before any of its resources are released. Its defining move is phase-boundary authorization on a schedule: passage from one stage to the next is never automatic, and momentum from completed work never carries into the next phase by default; each crossing must be re-earned against forward criteria. It becomes an escalation exit gate — rather than a completion checklist — precisely when the gate holds real authority to withhold the next phase and when it tests continuation against present evidence instead of merely confirming that the previous phase's tasks were finished.
## How it works¶

  * Chop the project into phases with a gate at each boundary. Work advances in stages, and every boundary is a decision, not a formality.
  * Set forward pass criteria before each phase. Each gate's criteria describe the evidence the phase must produce, not the tasks it must complete — evidence is what lets the gate deny a doomed but on-schedule project.
  * Staff the gate independently. The gatekeeper is separate from the delivery team and holds the authority to withhold the next phase.
  * Authorize or withhold at each gate. The outcome is passage to the next phase, or a withheld authorization that returns the work with conditions to re-present.
  * Recur at every boundary. The gates are a standing sequence; the review rhythm is the lifecycle itself.

## Tuning parameters¶

  * Number and placement of gates — more gates give tighter control and catch drift early, but multiply overhead and slow the lifecycle.
  * Criteria type — evidence-based versus completion-based. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Gate deliverables: Defined outputs from the previous Stage – such as research findings, technical results, financial analyses, and updated project plans – brought by the project team to support the decision. to verify that the product functions under actual use conditions, and also to measure purchase intent.

  * Trial, Limited, or Pilot Operations

to test, debug, and prove the operations process, and to determine more precise costs and throughputs.

  * Pretest Market, Test Market, or Trial Sell

to gauge customer reaction, measure the effectiveness of the launch plan, and determine expected market share and revenues.

### 3.10 Gate 5: Go to Launch

This final gate opens the door to full commercialization: market launch, and operations start-up. Criteria for passing the gate focus largely on the expected financial return, the project's readiness for launch, and the appropriateness of the launch and operations start-up plans.
